title: Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4)
hook: blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word of the sermon, blessed, and your line was empty hands can receive. Did you let someone help you? Day two hundred thirty-four.

Grief gets a polite schedule. A few days off work. A card. Then, gently, the world expects a person to be fine. People say, stay strong, or at least they're in a better place, and mean it kindly. But sometimes what a grieving person needs is someone who will let them be sad. The second line of Jesus's sermon goes somewhere few would expect. After the empty-handed, he congratulates the people who are crying.
screen: `GRIEF ON A POLITE SCHEDULE.` → `STAY STRONG.` → `THE SECOND LINE OF THE SERMON.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The Greek word for mourn, pentheo, is a word used for mourning the dead: grief that shows, not a quiet sigh. And Jesus doesn't say, blessed are those who get over it. He says, blessed are those who mourn. Christians have read this in a few ways. It's grief for someone you've lost. It's also grief over the wrong in the world, and over your own wrongs; some early Christian teachers read it that way. And the prophet Isaiah had promised one who would come to comfort all that mourn. Jesus seems to be saying: that's now. Here's the second word worth opening. Comforted in Greek is a form of parakaleo, which can mean to call to your side. It's the same family as the word John's Gospel uses for the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, which the King James Bible translates the Comforter. So comfort here isn't a pat on the back from across the room. It's someone called in to sit beside you. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say you won't mourn. It doesn't say your grief is wrong or weak. Jesus himself wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus. Paul later tells Christians not to sorrow as others which have no hope: not to stop sorrowing, but to sorrow with hope. That's the beatitude: grief that is real, and comfort promised to it. Mourning is not the end.
screen: `MOURN: GRIEF FOR THE DEAD.` · `FOR THE LOST, AND FOR THE WRONG.` · `COMFORT: CALLED TO YOUR SIDE.` · `GRIEF WITH HOPE.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone grieving. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who has lost something this year: a person, a marriage, a job, their health. Picture them. Don't plan a speech. Just ask yourself: what would it look like to sit beside them? A message that says, I'm thinking of you, no reply needed. A meal. A walk. Choose one. If you pray, you can name them before God. The bell holds the time.
Pentheo, the Greek word for mourn, grief that shows. The second beatitude: the ones who grieve out loud are blessed, because someone will come to their side.
Your line: mourning is not the end. Today, reach out to one grieving person, and don't try to fix it. Just come to their side. Day two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Christians keep funerals and memorial prayers for the dead, and some churches hold services for those grieving, especially around All Souls' Day or in the dark weeks before Christmas.

fork.setup: a friend is grieving hard, weeks after everyone else has moved on. what does the beatitude point you toward?
options: give them space until they're over it.
fork.reveal: comfort in Greek means called to your side. the beatitude doesn't hurry grief; it promises company in it.

original.note: Greek: they shall be comforted. from parakaleo, to call alongside; the Paraclete comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: blessed are those who get over it.
what it means: blessed are those who grieve out loud, for they shall be comforted.
what a scholar hears: comforted is parakaleo, called alongside, the root of Paraclete; the verse echoes Isaiah 61:2.

notes: pentheo as the strongest Greek word for grief (used for mourning the dead): common commentary claim; confirm.
Early Christian readings of mourning for sin (e.g. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 15): the script says 'many early Christian teachers'; confirm.
Isaiah 61:2 'to comfort all that mourn' and 1 Thessalonians 4:13 'sorrow not, even as others which have no hope' are paraphrased/partly echoed in the voice; not cited as quotations.
Parakaleo / parakletos family: confirm. 'Blue Christmas' / Longest Night services in howItsDone; confirm.
